notes.meaning: The list goes on with the family of Jerahmeel, Judah's great-grandson. Abishur's wife, Abihail, is named, and she had two sons, Ahban and Molid. Abishur's branch of the family ends with these two.

Nadab's line runs for four generations, down to Ahlai. Seled died without children, and Matthew Henry says such families are a comfort to people who are childless today. God gives or holds back children as he pleases, and he can be better to us than many sons. Ahlai is a puzzle, because verse 34 says Sheshan had no sons. Some think Ahlai was a daughter who carried on the family. Others think Ahlai was a son who died before his father.

Next comes the family of Jada, Shammai's brother. Jether also died without children, but his brother Jonathan had two sons. The line "these were the descendants of Jerahmeel" closes this part of the list.

Sheshan had only daughters, so he let his daughter marry Jarha, his Egyptian servant. An old Jewish paraphrase says Sheshan first set him free. The commentators think Jarha had turned to Israel's God and was a man of good character. Otherwise an Israelite would not have given him his daughter. Through this marriage Jarha was taken into Judah's tribe and became heir to the family. Matthew Henry notes that a person's birth or low position should not keep them back when they serve God well.
The family of Jarha and Sheshan's daughter is traced from father to son. It may have started in Egypt, where Sheshan probably owned Jarha. The line then went on into the land of Israel.

The line goes on to Elishama, thirteen generations in all. It probably reaches to near the end of the time of the judges. These names appear elsewhere in the Old Testament. But no one can show that any of those people belonged to this family.

This Caleb is the son of Hezron and brother of Jerahmeel. He is not the famous Caleb, son of Jephunneh, who spied out the land. These sons may have come from a third wife. "Father of Ziph" probably means the leader of the people of Ziph. The Geneva Notes say a ruler should care for his people like a father. The Hebrew of the second half of the verse is hard to follow.

Hebron's sons and grandsons are listed. Keil and Delitzsch argue that these are real people, not just towns, because the text speaks of fathers having sons. Beth-zur was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Jerusalem. Maon's family must have lived there.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have suggested that Mareshah and Hebron here are names of cities. On that view, the list shows how towns were linked rather than who fathered whom.

notes.meaning: Caleb also had children by Ephah, his concubine. A concubine was a lesser wife, taken without a wedding. Her children did not inherit the land, though they were given goods or money. Jahdai's family appears suddenly, and we are not told how he fits into the family tree.

Another concubine, Maacah, also had sons. Several of them are called "father" of towns in Judah, such as Madmannah. The list ends by naming Caleb's daughter Acsah. She is probably the well-known Acsah whom Caleb gave as a reward to the man who captured Debir. Here "daughter" may simply mean a later female descendant of this older Caleb.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Caleb son of Hezron and Caleb son of Jephunneh were really the same man. On that view, Acsah was his actual daughter.

notes.meaning: Next come the families from Hur, Caleb's son by Ephrathah. Men are called "father" of Kiriath-jearim, Bethlehem and Beth-gader. Their families settled those places and lived there. Bethlehem later became David's city and the birthplace of Christ. This Salma is a different man from the Salma in David's own family line.

Shobal's descendants include Haroeh, probably the Reaiah named in 1 Chronicles 4:2, and half of the Manahathites. They also include the clans of Kiriath-jearim. Two of David's mighty men later came from the Ithrites. From these clans also came the people of Zorah, Samson's hometown, and of Eshtaol.

Salma's descendants include the people of Bethlehem and of nearby Netophah, which later produced well-known men. Families of scribes, men skilled in writing and in God's law, lived at Jabez. They were Kenites, from the family of Moses' father-in-law. They are counted with Judah because they lived among Judah's people and married into them. Matthew Henry is glad to find families of Bible teachers among these great clans. He wishes every family were well taught in God's ways.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars, following the old Latin translation, read the three clan names as jobs, such as singers and those who live in tents. Others reject this and take them as family names.
